A low just east of Florida has a medium chance of becoming a tropical or subtropical storm. As of early Friday, November 20, the National Hurricane Center was giving it a 30% chance of developing within the next two days and a 50% chance within seven days. These temperatures are more than adequate to support tropical or subtropical development. Other environmental conditions may also become favorable for development as early as Friday, including relatively low wind shear. Figure 3. Sea surface temperatures in the low 80s east of Florida over the Gulf Stream. Notice the swath that remains in the 80s east of the mid-Atlantic. (Image credit: NOAA Ocean Prediction Center ) Reminder: A system does not need to become a named storm to produce significant impacts Whether this system receives an official name, it is likely to produce strong easterly winds, periods of heavy rainfall, rough surf, and potentially dangerous coastal conditions over an extensive area of the Eastern Seaboard. Melbourne, FL up to over 20" of rainfall for November, doubling the prior record for the month — and unsurprisingly the St. Johns River has reached record levels in the area. Bay Area of CA also setting rainfall records — and more to come in both regions. balancedweather.substack.com/p/heavy-rain… — Alan Gerard (@wxmanms1.bsky.social) 2026-11-19T18:10:07.196629Z Excessive rainfall is forecast to continue across the Space Coast tomorrow and bring significant to locally catastrophic flooding impacts. Have a way to receive warnings and never walk or drive into flooded roads. pic.twitter.com/vGIs2b5IMZ — NWS Weather Prediction Center (@NWSWPC) November 19, 2026 As this coastal storm tracks north-northeastward, heavy rainfall and gusty winds could eventually spread into the Northeast and New England throughout the weekend. Although models agree on this system’s general trajectory, a slight left or right shift could bring the center onshore along the Carolinas or keep it well offshore. Thus, residents along the Southeast coast should keep monitoring the forecast, as the system’s exact track, strength, and timing will determine where the most significant impacts occur. By October 2, the Atlantic basin averages its 11th named tropical system. By November 19, the basin typically has experienced approximately 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes. To refresh our memories, the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has produced only 10 named tropical storms. Only one has become a hurricane, Isaias, which was also the season’s only major hurricane. A significant coastal flood threat Strong onshore winds and 10-15-foot waves are expected to cause repeated rounds of minor to moderate coastal flooding and moderate to locally major beach erosion from Florida’s east coast north of the Bahamas into early Saturday, then extend northward into the coastal Carolinas over the weekend. If the storm hugs the North Carolina coast, this coastal flooding is likely to be particularly problematic in the Outer Banks, where coastal storms in September and October already washed out the only road connecting the vulnerable barrier island chain to the mainland, NC-12. The September nor’easter brought the fifth-highest water level since records began in 1979 at the NOAA tide gauge at Duck , located in the northern Outer Banks. The storm’s erosion caused multiple home collapses, with the Island Free Press reporting that the National Seashore beach in North Carolina suffered “a significant amount of private beach stairs and boardwalk decking, septic system parts, and wooden and metal debris from houses littering the beach.” The beach was closed because of human waste from the destroyed septic systems fouling the water. The September and October nor’easters caused 16 home collapses; before these storms, 32 houses collapsed into the ocean along the Outer Banks from 2020 to February 2026, for a total of 48 home collapses from 2020 to October 2026. The October nor’easter shut NC-12 for 10 days, and the road currently has just one lane open at the washout spot . A similar washout of NC-12 is possible from this weekend’s storm. Even if the Outer Banks escape a washout from this weekend’s storm, another coastal storm capable of inundating NC-12 is likely on Wednesday or Thursday, according to recent runs of the European and GFS models. This storm will be striking during the full moon king tide period, which will have unusually high tides. During the coming winter, we can expect that multiple strong nor’easters will affect the mid-Atlantic, and the prospects of multiple washouts of NC-12 through spring 2027 appear high. Figure 4. Sea level rise from 1979-2025 in Duck, North Carolina, was about 9.4 inches, of which 3.1 inches was from human-caused global warming. (Image credit: Climate Central ) High tide flooding will ramp up significantly in North Carolina in the next 10 years Storm erosion problems for the Outer Banks will get much, much worse in the next few decades. Between 1979 and 2025, sea level increased by about 9.4 inches at Duck, in the northern Outer Banks. About 33% of this increase can be confidently attributed to human-caused global warming, according to Climate Central. This acceleration in sea level rise has led to a sharp increase in high tide flooding over the past 20 years. What would have been a one-in-10-year flood in 1979 (2.64 feet above high tide) has already occurred on five days at Duck in 2026 . As I (Jeff Masters) wrote in my 2023 post, 30 great tools to determine your flood risk in the U.S. , a periodicity in the moon’s orbit causes much higher rates of sea level rise for different portions of the coast at different times during the next 18.6 years. An inflection point in this cycle came for Duck in 2023, and as a result, the next 10 or so years will see a sharp increase in the relative rate of sea level rise for the North Carolina Outer Banks. Over the past five years, Duck has averaged about 15 days per year with “minor” coastal flooding, as defined by the National Weather Service. Under an “Intermediate” scenario (the path that most closely approximates sea level rise at Duck over the past few decades), NOAA and NASA predict that by 2045, the Outer Banks will see 80 flood days per year — over one day per week. The king tide months of October, September, and November will have the highest risk of increased flooding. Not long after, these barrier islands are likely to suffer unofficial, gradual abandonment as rising sea levels and stronger storms fueled by human-caused climate change pound the coast. Kyle could form off Florida as extensive, prolonged coastal flood threat grows

by Irene Sans and Jeff Masters, Yale Climate Connections
November 19, 2026

If you thought the tropical season had wrapped up, don't bet on it just yet! Hurricane season is still on, and a tropical or subtropical storm could develop as soon as Friday, November 20, just east of Florida. Hurricane hunter flights have been scheduled to investigate this system beginning at midday Friday. The next name on the Atlantic list is Kyle.

Torrential rainfall this week in Southeast Florida has already caused numerous headaches, school closures, changes to work schedules, and endless road detours. Many neighborhoods, including Plantation, a Broward County suburb, have received more than 16 inches of rain, with over a foot falling between Tuesday and early Wednesday. Rain continued across parts of the area Thursday morning. These heavy rains were tied to a frontal system that will remain across the Florida Peninsula as mid-level energy slowly moves north along it, bringing torrential rainfall along the Space Coast and the I-95 corridor into Southeast Georgia.

One major uncertainty is whether this system will intensify far enough offshore to organize into Tropical or Subtropical Storm Kyle.

Record-to-near-record warm ocean temperatures off Florida's east coast have boosted extreme rains. Strong easterly surface winds have pushed very moist air from the Atlantic toward Florida's east coast. According to Climate Central’s Ocean Shift Index, human-caused climate change made near-record warmth in waters within about 200 miles of Florida's east coast two to seven times more likely.

How we could see Tropical or Subtropical Storm Kyle develop

As mid-level energy continues pushing north across the stalled front, a low-pressure system may develop near the surface over the unusually warm November waters just east of Florida. Assuming the system strengthens, it could become a subtropical or tropical storm while moving north-northeast, potentially hugging the Southeast U.S. coastline throughout the weekend.

One factor supporting potential development this weekend is the warm Gulf Stream. This powerful ocean current transports warm tropical water northward along the western Atlantic from near the Bahamas. Sea surface temperatures just east of Florida remain in the low 80s, while offshore waters along the southeastern United States range from the upper 70s to the low 80s. These temperatures are more than adequate to support tropical or subtropical development. Other environmental conditions may also become favorable for development as early as Friday, including relatively low wind shear.

Reminder: A system does not need to become a named storm to produce significant impacts

Whether this system receives an official name, it is likely to produce strong easterly winds, periods of heavy rainfall, rough surf, and potentially dangerous coastal conditions over an extensive area of the Eastern Seaboard. The greatest impacts could initially be felt along the I-95 corridor from Northeast Florida through Georgia and the Carolinas. The NOAA/NWS Weather Prediction Center has placed east-central Florida in and around the Space Coast in a high-risk area for Friday and Friday night (level 4 of 4) for potentially excessive rain leading to flooding.

For the period November 1-18, Melbourne International Airport had already racked up 17.25 inches of rain, and preliminary data shows that close to five additional inches had fallen by early afternoon on Thursday, November 19. If confirmed, this would not only push this month's rainfall well beyond double the city's record for any November (9.72 inches, set in 1963), but it would smash the city's record for any month (21.06 inches, set in August 2018) – with 11 full days left in the month and more rain in the forecast.

As this coastal storm tracks north-northeastward, heavy rainfall and gusty winds could eventually spread into the Northeast and New England throughout the weekend. Although models agree on this system's general trajectory, a slight left or right shift could bring the center onshore along the Carolinas or keep it well offshore. Thus, residents along the Southeast coast should keep monitoring the forecast, as the system's exact track, strength, and timing will determine where the most significant impacts occur.

By October 2, the Atlantic basin averages its 11th named tropical system. By November 19, the basin typically has experienced approximately 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes. To refresh our memories, the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has produced only 10 named tropical storms. Only one has become a hurricane, Isaias, which was also the season's only major hurricane.

A significant coastal flood threat

Strong onshore winds and 10-15-foot waves are expected to cause repeated rounds of minor to moderate coastal flooding and moderate to locally major beach erosion from Florida’s east coast north of the Bahamas into early Saturday, then extend northward into the coastal Carolinas over the weekend. If the storm hugs the North Carolina coast, this coastal flooding is likely to be particularly problematic in the Outer Banks, where coastal storms in September and October already washed out the only road connecting the vulnerable barrier island chain to the mainland, NC-12.

The September nor'easter brought the fifth-highest water level since records began in 1979 at the NOAA tide gauge at Duck, located in the northern Outer Banks. The storm's erosion caused multiple home collapses, with the Island Free Press reporting that the National Seashore beach in North Carolina suffered “a significant amount of private beach stairs and boardwalk decking, septic system parts, and wooden and metal debris from houses littering the beach.” The beach was closed because of human waste from the destroyed septic systems fouling the water.

The September and October nor'easters caused 16 home collapses; before these storms, 32 houses collapsed into the ocean along the Outer Banks from 2020 to February 2026, for a total of 48 home collapses from 2020 to October 2026. The October nor'easter shut NC-12 for 10 days, and the road currently has just one lane open at the washout spot. A similar washout of NC-12 is possible from this weekend’s storm. Even if the Outer Banks escape a washout from this weekend's storm, another coastal storm capable of inundating NC-12 is likely on Wednesday or Thursday, according to recent runs of the European and GFS models. This storm will be striking during the full moon king tide period, which will have unusually high tides. During the coming winter, we can expect that multiple strong nor'easters will affect the mid-Atlantic, and the prospects of multiple washouts of NC-12 through spring 2027 appear high.

High tide flooding will ramp up significantly in North Carolina in the next 10 years

Storm erosion problems for the Outer Banks will get much, much worse in the next few decades. Between 1979 and 2025, sea level increased by about 9.4 inches at Duck, in the northern Outer Banks. About 33% of this increase can be confidently attributed to human-caused global warming, according to Climate Central. This acceleration in sea level rise has led to a sharp increase in high tide flooding over the past 20 years. What would have been a one-in-10-year flood in 1979 (2.64 feet above high tide) has already occurred on five days at Duck in 2026.

As I (Jeff Masters) wrote in my 2023 post, 30 great tools to determine your flood risk in the U.S., a periodicity in the moon’s orbit causes much higher rates of sea level rise for different portions of the coast at different times during the next 18.6 years. An inflection point in this cycle came for Duck in 2023, and as a result, the next 10 or so years will see a sharp increase in the relative rate of sea level rise for the North Carolina Outer Banks.

The forecast for coastal flooding in North Carolina’s Outer Banks is truly intimidating. Over the past five years, Duck has averaged about 15 days per year with “minor” coastal flooding, as defined by the National Weather Service. Under an "Intermediate" scenario (the path that most closely approximates sea level rise at Duck over the past few decades), NOAA and NASA predict that by 2045, the Outer Banks will see 80 flood days per year — over one day per week. And if sea level rise increases to the "Intermediate High" range, by 2065, 90% of all days are predicted to see flooding.

Sea level rise is predicted to continue to accelerate into the next century. In past eras when sea level rise was as high as is expected by 2080-2100, barrier islands were rare because erosion was too high. In just a few years, it’s likely to become prohibitively expensive to maintain a road into the Outer Banks. Not long after, these barrier islands are likely to suffer unofficial, gradual abandonment as rising sea levels and stronger storms fueled by human-caused climate change pound the coast. With a permanent population of around 57,000, the Outer Banks don't have the tax base needed to fund the kind of adaptation efforts that will be needed to keep up with accelerating sea level rise.

Not just North Carolina is at risk from sea level rise

Beginning around 2033, the 18.6-year lunar cycle will significantly increase the rate of sea level rise and rapidly increase high-tide flooding along most of the Gulf of Mexico coast, portions of the Southeast Coast, the West Coast, and Hawaii. The rapid acceleration in coastal flooding simultaneously along a huge swathe of heavily developed U.S. coast by the mid-2030s will be sure to significantly stress the coastal housing market.
